Overview
From artificial hips, to LED screens, to wind turbines, to high-density computer memory, to lithium ion batteries, materials are foundational to all of today’s technological systems. Modern materials science and engineering (MSE) draws equally from scientific disciplines, such as chemistry, physics, molecular biology, and geosciences, and from application-focused engineering disciplines such as mechanical, chemical, electrical and civil, to synthesize its own identity and focus. Princeton Materials Institute (PMI) was established in 1990 with this interdisciplinary spirit, with founding members spanning science and engineering departments across campus. PMI now hosts nearly 100 associated faculty members from more than a dozen disciplines. Princeton’s national strength in materials research was recognized in 1994 with the award of a Materials Research Science and Engineering Center from the National Science Foundation, which has continued to this day as the Princeton Center for Complex Materials (PCCM), housed within PMI.

Ph.D.
Program description
The Ph.D. in MSE program at the Princeton Materials Institute builds on Princeton’s position as a leader in the study and design of advanced materials. This five-year program offers a doctoral degree to students with undergraduate training in materials and/or wish to be principally identified as materials scientists and engineers. The program leverages the wide array of PMI faculty members at the leading edge of many important research areas addressing innovations and solutions for today’s complex problems. Key features of the Ph.D. program include an interdisciplinary community, a collaborative environment, access to state-of-the-art material synthesis, characterization and simulation tools at PMI's Imaging & Analysis Center and Micro/Nanofabrication Center, access to Princeton Research Computing and weekly PMI/PCCM seminars.
Courses
Students will be required to take seven courses, plus a non-credit course on materials research at Princeton, and a half-term course on responsible conduct of research. Beyond an introductory course, the required curriculum consists of courses in three central topics within materials science and engineering (thermodynamics of materials, solid state structure and characterization, and kinetics and phase transformations in materials), plus a methods course (experimental or theoretical/computational), coupled with at least two courses in the student’s specific area of interest.
General exam
The general examination will consist of a written proposal and the student’s oral defense of it. The proposal will be based on the student’s chosen area of thesis research. This proposal defense will be considered together with a review of the student’s overall academic record and research progress. Completion of the five non-elective courses, with a minimum of a 3.0 average, is required to advance to the proposal defense; otherwise, degree candidacy will be terminated.
Students are expected to stand for the general examination during the January examination period of their second year of study.
The general examination committee will consist of three faculty, a maximum of two of whom will have the same primary departmental appointment. All examiners will have a PMI affiliation or the approval of the DGS to serve on the committee. If a student does not sustain the examination on the first attempt, a second attempt may be permitted in accordance with Graduate School policy, during the May examination period of the second year of study. Students passing the General Examination will qualify for the incidental Master of Arts (M.A.) degree.
Teaching
Students will be required to teach six contact hours per week for one term (one full-time assignment) or three contact hours per week for two terms (two half-time assignments); this requirement will typically be fulfilled during the second year of enrollment.
Post-Generals requirements
Yearly Committee Meetings
After a student completes the general exam, a yearly committee meeting is required for re-enrollment. This meeting is scheduled by the student. The committee consists of the adviser and two other PMI faculty members. The responsibility of the committee is to work with the adviser to help guide the student during their research. At the conclusion of each committee meeting, a brief summary and any recommendations will be provided by the committee to the student and the DGS. To facilitate students maintaining progress in formulating and meeting their goals through the Ph.D., students will also be encouraged to implement Individual Development Plans, and review these plans and the recommendations of their committee with their primary adviser and committee members.
Third Year Seminar
In the spring of their year of study, students will present a thirty-minute seminar on their research progress. To foster understanding of the different materials disciplines, all first-year and third-year students are required to attend all such seminars, and students from all years of enrollment will be invited.
Dissertation and FPO
The program’s recommendation to the University to award a Ph.D. is made after the candidate’s doctoral dissertation has been accepted and the final public oral examination sustained. The committee evaluating the FPO is typically the same committee that evaluates the student’s general examination, although changes in committee composition may be warranted (with the approval of the DGS) based on the specific research covered by time of the FPO.
